episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Thursday, April 16, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, a community college professor is warning that artificial intelligence represents an existential challenge for two-year institutions. Writing in The Bend Bulletin, Peter Magidson of Central Oregon Community College argues that traditional academic cycles are too slow to keep pace with A.I.-driven change. He describes what he calls a velocity gap, where curriculum that takes eighteen months to clear committees and accreditation becomes outdated before students even complete it. Whether teaching cybersecurity or training nurses on A.I. diagnostics, Magidson writes, eighteen months makes that knowledge a relic. He argues that schools are not selling an education but providing an expensive history lesson. Magidson also identifies what he calls a salary inversion. A qualified instructor might start at seventy thousand dollars, he notes, but the students they train often out-earn them within their first year. This creates a dangerous incentive structure that attracts those seeking a retirement job or a temporary stepping stone, and erodes educational quality when institutions cannot compete for top-tier talent. To survive, Magidson argues, community colleges must leverage A.I. to achieve parity with the private sector, then shift focus from what a student needs to know to what they must be able to do. The human advantage lies in what he calls the last mile of education: mentorship, tactile proficiency in hands-on troubleshooting, and local ecosystems that provide teamwork, networking, and the actual bridge to a paycheck.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Investing in Innovation, Howard University and Autodesk announced a one point nine five million dollar unrestricted donation to support the development of a construction engineering and management program in Howard's College of Engineering and Architecture. According to Howard University, the announcement coincides with the grand opening of a new thirty-four hundred square foot CEA Makerspace focused on A.I.-powered design and digital fabrication where students can transform ideas into prototypes. The donation builds on a 2024 gift of five million dollars from Autodesk, the largest unrestricted philanthropic gift in the college's history. Students will have access to A.I.-powered tools, industry-grade computer-aided engineering software, and virtual reality capabilities. The makerspace will also support outreach efforts designed to introduce younger students to STEM education. The construction industry in the United States represents nearly two trillion dollars in economic activity and faces a growing workforce shortage with hundreds of thousands of open roles projected annually over the next decade.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers, the University of Cincinnati's 1819 Innovation Hub has partnered with Tata Consultancy Services and Salesforce to create a direct pathway from classroom to A.I. jobs. According to the university, the new program called My First A.I. Job provides students with A.I. skills certification, paid work experience, and a pathway to full-time roles at TCS after graduation. The three-month intensive experience targets final-year students and will launch with a summer 2026 pilot through special topics information technology courses open to both undergraduate and graduate students. The goal is to ensure graduates can contribute to A.I.-driven workplaces from day one. Students will complete a Salesforce certification curriculum co-developed by the three partners and have the opportunity to participate in a fall co-op at TCS, gaining paid hands-on experience. TCS recently opened a Salesforce Center of Excellence at its Global Delivery Center in Milford, the company's largest U.S. delivery center.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, Arizona State University is adding a new fee to fund A.I. and technology tools. According to The Arizona Republic, the Arizona Board of Regents approved a one hundred dollar per semester fee on April 16. The fee applies to both undergraduate and graduate students each semester and is projected to generate roughly twenty-eight million dollars in annual revenue. The move signals ASU's latest investment in A.I. technology and innovation, joining a growing number of institutions implementing dedicated funding mechanisms for A.I. infrastructure.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And from Indiana University, GenAI 101 is now available to everyone worldwide at no cost. According to IU News, the course developed by faculty and staff at the IU Kelley School of Business has enrolled more than one hundred fourteen thousand students, staff, and faculty since launching in August. In October, IU expanded access to its more than eight hundred five thousand alumni worldwide. The self-paced course includes eight modules and sixteen concise lessons covering prompt engineering, data storytelling, fact-checking A.I.-generated content, and ethical A.I. use. It features an A.I. learning agent named Crimson that provides on-demand support for learners. Kelley School Dean Pat Hopkins cited data indicating ninety percent of employers are expected to implement A.I. solutions by 2028.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Thank you for joining us. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
